title: A Life Given in Their Place

memory_verse.label: Bible Reference
memory_verse.text: "Bring the bull to the front of the tent of meeting, and Aaron and his sons shall lay their hands on its head. Slaughter it in the Lord's presence at the entrance to the tent of meeting. Take some of the bull's blood and put it on the horns of the altar with your finger, and pour out the rest of it at the base of the altar." - Exodus 29:10-12 (NIV)

devotion.label: Devotion
devotion.text:
Aaron and his sons lay their hands on the bull's head before it is killed. This gesture mattered enormously. It signified transfer — the guilt of the one laying hands on the animal passing to the animal, which would then die in their place. They were not merely donating livestock. They were identifying with a substitute.

That laying on of hands is one of the clearest pictures of substitution in the Old Testament. Someone must bear the guilt. Either the sinner dies, or something dies in the sinner's place. God graciously provided the second option, and the hands on the head made the exchange personal and deliberate.

Isaiah would later write that the Lord laid on Him the iniquity of us all (Isa 53:6) — the same image, now fulfilled in a Person rather than an animal. Paul puts it starkly: God made Him who had no sin to be sin for us, so that in Him we might become the righteousness of God (2 Cor 5:21). Christ is the substitute upon whom our guilt was laid. When you think of the cross, picture those hands pressing down. Your guilt did not evaporate; it was transferred, and He bore it.

reflection.label: Reflection
reflection.text:
Do I truly grasp that my guilt was transferred to Christ, not merely overlooked?
How does the reality of substitution change how I view the cross?

prayer.label: Prayer
prayer.text: Lord Jesus, my guilt was not ignored but laid upon You. Thank You for bearing what I deserved. Let the wonder of that exchange never grow ordinary to me. Amen.
